# Introduction {-}
We will look at linear regression and compare some other AI methods to analyze the Heart data. In this notebook we will introduce one-hot coding for the categorical drivers, and build the models with this encoded data. 

# Packages {-}

Loading the standard packages for this course:
```{r}
library(tidyverse) # used to manipulate data and plot
library(ISLR2) #package contains the data files, but not this one
library(ggfortify) # some extra ggplot functions
library(GGally) # pairs ggplot and other options
library(flextable) # nice displays of printed data
library(DT) #more nice table displays from RStudio
library(broom) # neat model summary
library(car) # useful tools for regression analysis
library(MASS) # for LDA analysis
library(class) # for knn analysis
library(caret) # for confusion matrix and for crossvalidation
library(mltools) # collection of machine learning tools
```

# Data {-}

We will load the Heart data from a csv file in the data folder.  We will use the Import Dataset button in the upper right panel. We will be sure to copy the code generated and place it in the notebook, so the notebook can run on its own.

```{r message=FALSE}
library(readr)
Heart <- read_csv("~/stfrancis/MBAD640 Data Mining/Course Files MBAD 640/Data Sets/Heart.csv")
Heart %>% glimpse
Heart
```

You can see that the first column has a funny name.  It seems to just count the observations, all 303 of  them.  Let's change the name of the first column to <code>Obs</code> for observation.
```{r}
names(Heart)[1]="Obs"
Heart
```

# Data Description {-}
It is always a good idea to run a <code>summary()</code> of the data.
```{r}
Heart %>% summary
```

# Data Wrangling {-}

There are some missing data. There are several character variables that should be turned into factors, and some 0-1 variables that should also be factors. 

```{r}
Heart = Heart %>% na.omit
Heart = Heart %>% mutate(Thal = factor(Thal), AHD=factor(AHD), ChestPain = factor(ChestPain),
                 Sex = factor(Sex), Fbs=factor(Fbs), ExAng=factor(ExAng),
                 RestECG = factor(RestECG), Slope=factor(Slope), Ca=factor(Ca)
)
Heart %>% glimpse
Heart %>% sapply(class) %>% enframe
```

# One-Hot Encoding

For machine learning applications it is helpful to make factor drivers into multiple dummy variables. This process is called one-hot encoding.  If a factor has $n$ levels, there will be $n$ dummy variables created, one for each level of the factor. The dataset can then be treated as all numeric.  The disadvantage is there are many more drivers, but faster computers and better algorithms handle that nicely.

We will create a one-hot encoded version of the data. the right function is in the <code>mltools</code> package.

```{r}
Heartoh = Heart %>% as.data.table %>% one_hot
Heartoh %>% glimpse
```
There are now 31 columns, and all the dummy columns can be seen as separate drivers.

```{r}
Heartoh %>% summary
Heartoh %>% glimpse
Heartoh %>% 
```

# Research Problem {-}
The research problem is to compare predictions of RestBP from the other variables, using linear regression and other AI methods. 

We will compare accuracy of the methods using root-mean squared error or RMSE, which can be computed from the predictions and the actual values of RestBP in the dataset. Note that we cannot compare AI methods directly with linear regression using anova, since the methods use totally different techniques.

# Data Visualization
We plot RestBP with some other variables.
```{r}
Heart %>% dplyr::select(where(is.numeric) & !contains("Obs")) %>% 
  ggpairs(progress=F)
```

We see some dependency of RestBP (second row and column) n the others, but it's hard to find a pattern.

Next we try the non-numeric factor variables. No correlation coefficients can be computed.

```{r fig.width=10}
Heart %>% dplyr::select(where(is.factor) & !contains("Obs")) %>% 
  ggpairs(progress=F)
```
Not pretty, but shows relative proportions of each variable with the others. Hard to read.

# Wrangling for Analysis (deprecated)

For our analysis we need all the data to be numeric.  We will convert all the factor variables to numeric.  Columns with several values will be converted to several consecutive integer values; binary factors will be converted to 1-2.

```{r}
Heartall = Heart %>% 
  dplyr::select(!contains("Obs")) %>% 
  sapply(FUN= as.numeric) %>% data.frame
Heartall
```

All columns are now numeric.

We will save this numeric data for use elsewhere.

```{r}
saveRDS(Heartall, file="Heartall.rds")
```

For analysis we will use the one-hot encoded dataframe <code>Heartoh</code>.

# Analysis {-}

We will use linear regression first.

## Linear Regression {-}

As a measure of accuracy we are going to use RMSE. The mltools package has functions for computing most of the common measures. 

```{r}
fit.lm.all = lm(RestBP~.-Obs, data=Heartoh)
fit.lm.all %>% summary %>% tidy() %>% mutate(" "=pvstars(fit.lm.all), .after=p.value)
fit.lm.all %>% summary %>% glance()
fit.lm.all %>% autoplot(which=1:3)
```

The QQ plot looks pretty good [References] [1]. There is an upward trend in the SL plot of residuals. Many drivers do not have significant coefficients. Adjusted R-squared is only 14.7%. Compute the accuracy.

```{r}
accuracy.rmse.lm.all = mltools::rmse(predict(fit.lm.all, newdata=Heartoh), Heartoh$RestBP)
accuracy.rmse.lm.all
```

The RMSE is `r accuracy.rmse.lm.all`. 

### Visualization

We make a plot of the corresponding fitted RestBP predictions against the actual RestBP numbers. We put in a line which denotes an exact match. This is NOT a conventional linear fit plot; there are four drivers, so we could not do that.  We could also plot the residuals against the fitted values; departure from zero would display the differences.

```{r}
plot.lm.all = ggplot(Heartoh) +
  geom_point(aes(RestBP, fit.lm.all$fitted.values))+
  geom_abline(aes(slope=1, intercept=0), color="blue", linetype="dashed", linewidth=1) +
  theme_bw() + 
  labs(title="RestBP vs Fitted Values",
       subtitle="Linear Regression, all drivers, one-hot encoding",
       x="Actual RestBP (mmHg)", y="Fitted RestBP")
plot.lm.all
```

## Neural Network {-}

For a neural network it is important to scale the variables, like to a 0-1 range. We do this by taking each value and subtracting from it the minimum of the column, then dividing by max - min of the column. When we get predictions, we will have to unscale them to compare them to the linear model.

```{r}
Heartoh.scaled = Heartoh %>% sapply(FUN = function (x) {
  (x-min(x))/(max(x)-min(x))})  %>% data.frame
Heartoh.scaled %>% glimpse
```
Run 3 repetitions of the same neural net.

```{r}
library(neuralnet)
fit.nn.all= neuralnet(RestBP~.-Obs, data=Heartoh.scaled, linear.output=F,
                      hidden=c(5,3), rep=3)
```

Display the neuralnet.

```{r fig.height=7, fig.width=10}
fit.nn.all %>% plot(rep='best')
```

It's a busy plot on the left because there are so many drivers. Make predictions and unscale them.

```{r}
pred.nn.all = predict(fit.nn.all, newdata=Heartoh.scaled)
pred.nn.all %>% summary
pred.nn.all.unscaled = min(Heartoh$RestBP) + (max(Heartoh$RestBP)-min(Heartoh$RestBP))*pred.nn.all
pred.nn.all.unscaled %>% summary
```

Compute accuracy now.

```{r}
accuracy.rmse.nn.all = mltools::rmse(pred.nn.all.unscaled, Heartoh$RestBP)
accuracy.rmse.nn.all
```

All the drivers give an RMSE of `r accuracy.rmse.nn.all`.

### Visualization

All drivers including discrete ones.

```{r}
plot.nn.all = ggplot(Heartoh) +
  geom_point(aes(RestBP, pred.nn.all.unscaled))+
  geom_abline(aes(slope=1, intercept=0), color="blue", linetype="dashed", linewidth=1) +
  theme_bw() + 
  labs(title="RestBP vs Fitted Values",
       subtitle="Neural Network, all drivers, one-hot encoding",
       x="Actual RestBP (mmHg)", y="Fitted RestBP")
plot.nn.all
```

### Generalized weights

We often use a generalized weights plot to see how the repetitions of the neural network are predicting. We will plot weights for the best repetition. Here's how the generalized weights plot is created. First we plot a ggplot version.

```{r}
# handmade generalized weights plot
best=which.min(fit.nn.all$result.matrix[1,])
gw2 = fit.nn.all$generalized.weights[[best]][,2] # Chol is the second variable
ggplot()+
  geom_point(aes(x=Heartoh.scaled$Chol,y=gw2)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,2)) +
  labs(title="Response: RestBP")+
  theme_bw()

# built-in generalized weights plot
gwplot(fit.nn.all, selected.covariate="Chol", rep='best')
```

Generalized weights cannot be compared with the coefficients of a linear model.

### Making Predictions with neural network

There are 3 repetitions. Each can make a separate prediction. We do them all together.

```{r message=FALSE}
# create all predictions
z = prediction(fit.nn.all)

#put them in a data frame, and compute errors, changing data column name to Actual
q = z %>% data.frame %>% 
  select(rep1.RestBP, rep2.RestBP, rep3.RestBP, data.RestBP) %>% 
  rename(Actual=data.RestBP) %>% 
  mutate(e1=rep1.RestBP-Actual,
         e2=rep2.RestBP-Actual,
         e3=rep3.RestBP-Actual) # compute the residuals for the three repetitions
q %>% boxplot()

# histograms of errors show the distributions, with a normal distribution overlaid
gh1 = ggplot(q, aes(x=e1))+
  geom_histogram(aes(y=after_stat(density)),
                 color="black", alpha=.3, fill="red") +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean=mean(q$e1), sd=sd(q$e1)))

gh2 = ggplot(q, aes(x=e2))+
  geom_histogram(aes(y=after_stat(density)),
                 color="black", alpha=.3, fill="blue") +
   stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean=mean(q$e2), sd=sd(q$e2)))
# gh2

gh3 = ggplot(q, aes(x=e3))+
  geom_histogram(aes(y=after_stat(density)), 
                 color="black", alpha=.3, fill="tan")+
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean=mean(q$e3), sd=sd(q$e3)))

# put the three histograms together
new('ggmultiplot', nrow=1, plots=list(gh1, gh2, gh3))
```

The errors look essentially normally distributed. Remember when explaining that the results will be different each time you run it, because the starting weights are seeded randomly.

## Random Forest

We will use a random forest AI method to model the hypothesis. It uses a random selection of 500 repetitions of many decision trees to create the best predictions.  It might not do as well next time, but might also do better. How do you explain that to the client? We perform the random forest model on all variables, making them numeric.Run the model.

```{r}
library(randomForest)
fit.rf.all = randomForest(RestBP~.-Obs, data=Heartoh, type="regression")
fit.rf.all %>% print
pred.rf.all = predict(fit.rf.all, newdata=Heartoh)
pred.rf.all %>% summary
```

Compute accuracy.

```{r}
accuracy.rmse.rf.all = mltools::rmse(pred.rf.all, Heartoh$RestBP)
accuracy.rmse.rf.all
```

The accuracy is `r accuracy.rmse.rf.all`.

### Visualization

```{r}
plot.rf.all = ggplot(Heartoh) +
  geom_point(aes(RestBP, pred.rf.all))+
  geom_abline(aes(slope=1, intercept=0), color="blue", linetype="dashed", linewidth=1) +
  theme_bw() + 
  labs(title="RestBP vs Fitted Values",
       subtitle="Random Forest, all drivers, one-hot encoded",
       x="Actual RestBP (mmHg)", y="Fitted RestBP")
plot.rf.all
```

The random forest seems biased to forecast low values too high and high values too low. A good fit should be right on the dotted line. It's a much more focused than the neural network.

## K-nearest neighbors

This model can also be used; the best version comes from package <code>FNN</code>.  We try it using 3 nearest neighbors, the value of parameter 'k'. We scale the data, though that should not be necessary. Now we try all variables.

```{r}
library(FNN)
fit.knn.all<- knn.reg(Heartoh.scaled %>% select(-RestBP, -Obs), y=Heartoh.scaled$RestBP, k=3)
pred.kk.all.unscaled = mean(Heartoh$RestBP) + fit.knn.all$pred*sd(Heartoh$RestBP)
```

Now compute the RMSE accuracy measure. 

```{r}
accuracy.rmse.kk.all = mltools::rmse(pred.kk.all.unscaled, Heartall$RestBP)
accuracy.rmse.kk.all
```

Not good.

### Visualization

```{r}
plot.kk.all = ggplot(Heartoh) +
  geom_point(aes(RestBP, pred.kk.all.unscaled))+
  geom_abline(aes(slope=1, intercept=0), color="blue", linetype="dashed", linewidth=1) +
  theme_bw() + 
  labs(title="RestBP vs Fitted Values",
       subtitle="3-Nearest Neighbors Regression, all drivers, one-hot encoding",
       x="Actual RestBP (mmHg)", y="Fitted RestBP")
plot.kk.all
```

Not so good either.

# Comparing the Models

## Accuracy

First compare accuracies.

```{r}
library(DT)
AccuracyComparisonAllOH = data.frame(OLS = accuracy.rmse.lm.all,
                                NNET = accuracy.rmse.nn.all,
                                RF = accuracy.rmse.rf.all,
                                KNN = accuracy.rmse.kk.all) %>% 
  round(digits=4)
AccuracyComparisonAllOH %>% mutate(Measure = "RMSE", .before=1) %>% 
  DT::datatable(caption="Accuracy Comparison, all drivers, one-hot encoding")
```

The neural net does well, but the random forest is better.

We save this comparison table for use with other AI routines.

```{r}
saveRDS(AccuracyComparisonAllOH, file = "AccuracyComparisonAllOH.rds")
```


## Visualizations

Now for all variables.

```{r}
new('ggmultiplot', ncol=2, plots = list(plot.lm.all,
                                        plot.nn.all + ggtitle(""), 
                                        plot.rf.all + ggtitle(""), 
                                        plot.kk.all + ggtitle(""))
)
```

# Conclusion {-}

We used the Heart data to fit models using linear regression and some AI methods, a neural network and a random forest, and k-nearest neighbors regression.  

With this data, the random forest gave the best fit, using RMSE as an accuracy measure. However we can see the bias in the results, predicting too high for low actual RestBP and too low for high RestBP. So the random forest might not be so useful.

The neural network had a lot of errors when it predicted around 130, though it was better above and below. We might want to explore a different hidden layer structure.

We also saw that the random forest method seemed to have a bias. The linear model, by design, did not; the mistakes it made were equally on each side, above or below.  Neither did the neural network.  Can we find a way to take the bias out of the random forest, to take advantage of its closer predictions?

Ideally we should do this experiment using crossvalidation, by dividing the dataset into two parts, training on the first part, and testing (predicting) on the second part. More about that later in the class. We need to do that because the AI methods use randomness in their processes, and you don't get the same result each time. Also we want the model to be *robust*, be able to make predictions on data it has not been trained on.  Crossvalidation is perfect for that.
